content: Water is used for survival, as coolant, solvent, for steam generation, air conditioning, fire-fighting and domestic purposes.

**Rainwater**: purest natural form, but dissolves CO₂, SO₂, NO₂. **Sea water**: ~3.5% dissolved salts, ~2.6% NaCl. **River water**: organic matter plus sulfates, bicarbonates, bromides of Na, K, Mg. **Lake water**: purer but rich in organic matter. **Underground water**: little suspended matter, high dissolved minerals.

(a) Dissolution of NaCl, gypsum. (b) Hydration:

> CaSO₄ + 2H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O (anhydrite → gypsum)

> Mg₂SiO₄ + xH₂O → Mg₂SiO₄·xH₂O (olivine → serpentine)

(c) Oxidation: 2Fe₃O₄ → 2Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe₂O₃·2H₂O (magnetite → haematite → limonite). (d) Action of CO₂:

> CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂

Hardness prevents lather formation with soap, caused by salts of Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺.

> 2C₁₇H₃₅COONa + CaCl₂ → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca↓ + 2NaCl

**Temporary hardness**: bicarbonates of Ca, Mg; removed by boiling. **Permanent hardness**: chlorides and sulfates; not removed by boiling.

> Ca(HCO₃)₂ →(heat) CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂

Expressed as ppm of CaCO₃ (mol. wt. 100, eq. wt. 50).

> CaCO₃ equivalent = mass of hardness-producing substance × 50 / chemical equivalent of the substance

> 1 ppm = 1 part hardness / 10⁶ parts water

> 1 °Fr = 1 part / 10⁵ parts water
> 1 °Clark = 1 grain / gallon (70,000 grains)
> 1 °USA = 1 grain / 58,300 grains
> 1 °German = 1 grain / 56,000 grains

**Domestic**: wasted soap, sticky precipitates, scum in cooking vessels, fuel wastage, poor tea/coffee taste, risk of calcium oxalate deposits. **Industrial**: textile/dyeing (deposits, iron stains), sugar refining, paper finish, laundry, concrete hydration, pharmaceuticals, boilers (scale, corrosion, priming/foaming, caustic embrittlement).

topic: 8. Sludge and Scale Formation in Boilers
content:
Salts saturate on continuous evaporation and deposit where flow is slow.

**Sludge**: loose, slimy precipitate (MgCO₃, MgSO₄, MgCl₂, CaCl₂), removed by brushing. **Scale**: hard adherent deposit. Causes: CaCO₃ from Ca(HCO₃)₂ (low pressure); CaSO₄ (solubility falls at high temperature); CaSiO₃/MgSiO₃; Mg(OH)₂.

> Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ (scale) + H₂O + CO₂

**Disadvantages of scale**: poor heat transfer (fuel use rises from ~50% to 150% as thickness goes 1.25→12 mm), overheating and unsafe operation, possible explosion, clogged valves. **Removal**: wooden/wire brush, blow-down, thermal shocks, 5–10% HCl or EDTA treatment.

(a) Colloidal conditioning (kerosene, tannin, agar-agar). (b) Phosphate conditioning:

> 3CaCl₂ + 2Na₃PO₄ → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 6NaCl

(c) Carbonate conditioning:

> CaSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ = CaCO₃ + Na₂SO₄

(d) Calgon conditioning: 2CaSO₄ + [Na₄P₆O₁₈]²− → [Ca₂P₆O₁₈]²− + 2Na₂SO₄. (e) Sodium aluminate. (f) Electrical. (g) Radioactive conditioning.

Cracking of stressed boiler parts (rivets, bends) by NaOH:

> Na₂CO₃ + H₂O → 2NaOH + CO₂

A concentration cell forms between Fe at rivets (+) in concentrated NaOH and Fe at plane surfaces (−) in dilute NaOH.
Use sodium phosphate instead of Na₂CO₃; add Na₂SO₄ (ratio Na₂SO₄/NaOH > 2.5); add tannin/lignin; use crack-resistant steel.

(a) Dissolved O₂ (8 ml/l at room temp):

> 2Fe + 2H₂O + O₂ → 2Fe(OH)₂↓

Removed by deaeration, or by hydrazine/sodium sulfite. (b) Dissolved CO₂ causes pitting:

> Fe + CO₂ + H₂O → FeCO₃ + H₂

Removed by mechanical deaeration, lime or NH₃, heating. (c) Mineral acids:

> MgCl₂ + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl; Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂
**Priming**: wet-steam carry-over, caused by dissolved solids, high steam velocity, sudden boiling. **Foaming**: stable bubbles caused by oil; reduced with anti-foaming agents.

Three methods: (1) lime-soda, (2) permutit/zeolite, (3) ion-exchange. **Lime-soda process** removes both hardnesses:

> Ca(HCO₃)₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2CaCO₃↓ + 2H₂O
> MgCO₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → Mg(OH)₂↓ + CaCO₃↓

> CaSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄

Chemicals, coagulant and water are stirred in a tank; sludge settles and water is filtered. Residual Ca hardness ≈ 40 ppm.

*Figure: Fig. 17.1 Continuous cold lime-soda softener (motor, stirrer, wood-fibre filter, sludge outlet) (see textbook)*

Water heated near boiling: faster, near-complete reaction, rapid settling, no coagulant, gases removed, lower residual hardness. Drawbacks: much sludge, unsuitable for high-pressure boilers.

*Figure: Fig. 17.2 Continuous hot lime-soda softener (reaction tank, conical sedimentation tank, sand filter) (see textbook)*

Zeolite = hydrated sodium aluminosilicate Na₂O·Al₂O₃·xSiO₂·yH₂O (natrolith). Hard water passes through a zeolite bed; Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ exchange for Na.

> Na₂Ze + Ca(HCO₃)₂ = 2NaHCO₃ + CaZe
> Na₂Ze + CaCl₂ = 2NaCl + CaZe

**Regeneration** with brine:

> CaZe + 2NaCl = Na₂Ze + CaCl₂

*Figure: Fig. 17.3 Softening by permutit process (see textbook)*

Advantages: hardness down to ~10 ppm, no sludge, easy to regenerate. Disadvantages: turbid or acidic water unsuitable; soft water contains NaHCO₃.

Cation resins (RH⁺) exchange H⁺; anion resins (ROH−) exchange OH−.

*Figure: Structures of cation exchange resin (–SO₃H) and anion exchange resin (–CH₂NMe₂⁺OH−) (see textbook)*

> 2RH⁺ + Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ → R₂Ca²⁺/R₂Mg²⁺ + 2H⁺
> ROH− + Cl− → R⁺Cl− + OH−

H⁺ and OH− combine to give deionized water.

*Figure: Fig. 17.4 Demineralisation of water (cation exchanger, anion exchanger, acid and alkaline regenerators) (see textbook)*

*Figure: Fig. 17.5 Ion exchanges during demineralisation (see textbook)*

**Regeneration**: cation resin with dil. H₂SO₄/HCl, anion resin with dil. NaOH.

> R₂Ca²⁺ + 2H⁺ → 2RH⁺ + Ca²⁺
Single cylinder with cation and strong anion resin; residual hardness ~1 ppm.

Drinking water: clear, odourless, no bad taste, suspended matter < 10 ppm, pH ≈ 8, dissolved salts < 500 ppm, free of pathogens. Steps: aeration, settling, sedimentation with coagulants (alum, green vitriol), filtration.

(i) Bleaching powder (1 kg per 1000 kilolitres):

> Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂; Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl

(ii) Break-point chlorination: chlorine is added until residual free chlorine appears; 0.3–0.5 ppm suffices.

(iii) Chloramine (Cl₂:NH₃ = 2:1 by volume):

> Cl₂ + NH₃ → Cl.NH₂ + HCl

(iv) **Ozonization**: O₃ gives nascent oxygen; no taste or odour; contact 10–15 min at 2–3 ppm; costly. Physical methods: boiling, sunlight, UV.
> SO₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O = 2HCl + H₂SO₄

(a) **Electrodialysis**: direct current drives Na⁺ to the cathode and Cl− to the anode through selective membranes.

*Figure: Fig. 17.6 Line diagram of electrodialysis (see textbook)*

*Figure: Fig. 17.7 Electrodialysis cell (alternate cation/anion selective membranes) (see textbook)*

(b) **Reverse osmosis**: pressure above osmotic pressure pushes solvent across a semipermeable membrane (cellulose acetate, polyamide).

1. Free chlorine: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂; titrate I₂ with N/50 hypo, starch indicator.

> Strength of free chlorine = V × 35.5 × 10⁶ / (2500 × 1000) ppm

2. Alkalinity: OH− + H⁺ → H₂O; CO₃²− + H⁺ → HCO₃−; HCO₃− + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.

Titrate 100 ml sample with N/50 H₂SO₄: phenolphthalein end point V₁, then methyl orange, extra V₂.

> P = V₁ × 50 × 10⁶ / (50 × 100 × 1000) ppm
> M = (V₁ + V₂) × 50 × 10⁶ / (50 × 100 × 1000) ppm

> Temporary hardness = (V₁ − V₂) × 10⁶ / (50 × 1000) ppm
> Permanent hardness = (50 − V) × 10⁶ / (50 × 1000) ppm

(ii) EDTA (disodium salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is a complexing agent for Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺.

Erichrome black T indicator, pH 10 (NH₄OH/NH₄Cl buffer); colour changes wine red → blue at end point.

Softening: lime-soda, zeolite, ion-exchange. Desalination: electrodialysis, reverse osmosis. Units: ppm, mg/l, °Clark (1 ppm = 0.07 °Cl), °French (1 ppm = 0.1 °Fr).
